source_text: Παίζων δ᾿, ὡς οἴεται, τὸν Ἰησοῦν ὁ παρὰ τῷ Κέλσῳ Ἰουδαῖος εἰδέναι ἀναγέγραπται τὸν Εὐριπίδου Βάκχον λέγοντα· λύσει μ᾿ ὁ δαίμων αὐτὸς, ὅταν ἐγὼ θέλω. οὐ πάνυ μὲν οὖν Ἰουδαῖοι τὰ Ἑλλήνων φιλολογοῦσιν. ἀλλ᾿ ἔστω τινὰ τῶν Ἰουδαίων καὶ φιλόλογον οὕτω γεγονέναι· πῶς οὖν ὁ Ἰησοῦς, ἐπεὶ μὴ ἔλυσεν αὑτὸν δεδεμένον. οὐδὲ ἐδύνατο λῦσαι; ἦ γὰρ ἐκ τῶν ἐμῶν γραφῶν πιστευέτω ὅτι καὶ Πέτρος δεδεμένος ἐν φυλακῇ ἀγγέλου λύσαντος τοὺς δεσμοὺς ἐξῆλθε, καὶ Παῦλος μετὰ τοῦ Σίλα ἐν Φιλίπποις τῆς Μακεδονίας ὑπὸ „ξύλον“ δεδεμένος ἐλύθη θείᾳ δυνάμει, ὅτε καὶ „θύραι“ τῆς φυλακῆς „ἠνοίχθησαν“. ἀλλ᾿ εἰκὸς ὅτι ταῦτα γελᾷ ὁ Κέλσος ἢ καὶ οὐδαμῶς ἀνέγνω τὴν ἱστορίαν· ἔδοξε γὰρ ἂν λέγειν πρὸς αὐτὴν ὅτι καὶ γόητές τινες ἐπῳδαῖς δεσμοὺς λύουσι καὶ θύρας ἀνοίγουσιν, ἵνα κοινοποιήσῃ τὰ τῶν γοήτων πρὸς τὰ παρ᾿ ἡμῖν ἱστορούμενα. ἀλλ᾿ οὐδ᾿ ὁ καταδικάσας. φησὶν. αὐτὸν ἔπαθέ τι. οἷον ὁ Πενθεὺς μανεὶς ἢ σπαραχθείς. οὐκ εἶδε δ᾿ ὅτι οὐχ οὕτω Πιλᾶτος ἦν καταδικάσας αὐτὸν, ὅς γε „ᾔδει ὅτι διὰ φθόνον παρέδωκαν αὐτὸν“ οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι, ὡς τὸ Ἰουδαίων ἔθνος· ὅπερ καταδεδίκασται ὑπὸ θεοῦ σπαραχθὲν καὶ εἰς πᾶσαν τὴν γῆν ὑπὲρ τὸν Πενθέως σπαραγμὸν διασπαρέν. διὰ τί δὲ καὶ ἑκὼν παρεπέμψατο τὰ περὶ τῆς γυναικὸς Πιλάτου. ἑωρακυίας ὄναρ καὶ οὕτω κεκινημένης ὑπ᾿ αὐτοῦ, ὡς προσπέμψαι τῷ ἀνδρὶ καὶ λέγειν· „μηδέν σοι καὶ τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ τούτῳ τῷ δικαίῳ· σήμερον γὰρ κατ᾿ ὄναρ πολλὰ ἔπαθον δι᾿ αὐτόν“; πάλιν τε αὖ σιωπῶν τὰ ἐμφαίνοντα τὴν τοῦ Ἰησοῦ θειότητα ὁ Κέλσος ὀνειδίζει ἐκ τῶν γεγραμμένων ἐν τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ περὶ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ. παρατιθέμενος τοὺς ἐμπαίξαντας αὐτῷ καὶ φοινικίδα περιθέντας καὶ τὸν ἐξ ἀκανθῶν στέφανον καὶ τὸν ἐν τῇ χειρὶ κάλαμον. πόθεν οὖν. ὦ Κέλσε. ταῦτα μεμάθηκας ἢ ἀπὸ τῶν εὐαγγελίων; ἆρ᾿ οὖν σὺ μὲν ἑώρας ταῦτα ὀνειδισμοῦ ἄξια, οἱ δ᾿ ἀναγράφοντες αὐτὰ οὐ κατενόουν ὅτι σὺ μὲν καταγελάσῃ καὶ οἱ σοὶ παραπλήσιοι ἄλλοι δὲ παράδειγμα λήψονται τοῦ καταφρονεῖν γελώντων καὶ χλευαζόντων ἐπὶ εὐσεβείᾳ τὸν δι᾿ αὐτὴν ἑτοίμως ἀποθανόντα; μᾶλλον οὖν θαύμαζε αὐτῶν τὸ φιλάληθες καὶ τοῦ ταῦτα ἑκουσίως παθόντος ὑπὲρ ἀνθρώπων καὶ μετὰ πάσης ἀνεξικακίας καὶ μακροθυμίας αὐτὰ ὑπομείναντος· οὐ γὰρ ἀνεγέγραπτο ὅτι ὠδύρατο ἤ τι ἀγεννὲς ἐκ τοῦ καταδεδικάσθαι ἐνομίσθη (ἢ) ἀνεφθέγξατο.
pass_a_gloss: Making sport of (παίζω), as he thinks, Jesus, the Jew in Celsus is written up (ἀναγράφω) as knowing Euripides' Bacchus saying: 'the god (δαίμων) himself will loose (λύω) me whenever I will (θέλω).' Not very much do Jews study (φιλολογέω) the things of Greeks; but let some Jew have become so literary (φιλόλογος): how then Jesus, since he did not loose himself bound (δέω), could not loose either? For let him believe from my scriptures (γραφαί) that Peter too, bound in prison (φυλακή), came out an angel (ἄγγελος) loosing the bonds (δεσμός), and Paul with Silas in Philippi of Macedonia bound under 'the wood (ξύλον)' was loosed by divine power (θεία δύναμις), when also 'doors' of the prison 'were opened'. But likely (εἰκός) Celsus laughs (γελάω) at these or never read (ἀναγινώσκω) the history (ἱστορία); for he would have seemed to say against it that some sorcerers (γόης) by incantations (ἐπῳδή) loose bonds and open doors, so as to make common (κοινοποιέω) the sorcerers' things with those recorded among us. 'But not even he who condemned (καταδικάζω),' he says, 'him suffered anything, like Pentheus maddened (μαίνομαι) or torn apart (σπαράσσω).' He did not see that not so much Pilate had condemned him, who 'knew that through envy (φθόνος) they handed him over (παραδίδωμι)', the Jews, as the nation (ἔθνος) of the Jews; which has been condemned by God, torn apart and scattered (διασπείρω) into all the earth beyond the tearing (σπαραγμός) of Pentheus. Why did he willingly (ἑκών) pass over (παραπέμπω) the things about Pilate's wife, having seen a dream (ὄναρ) and so moved (κινέω) by it as to send to her husband and say: 'nothing to you and to this righteous (δίκαιος) man; for today in a dream I suffered many things because of him'? Again, silent about things showing (ἐμφαίνω) Jesus' divinity (θειότης), Celsus reproaches (ὀνειδίζω) from things written in the gospel about Jesus, setting forth those who mocked (ἐμπαίζω) him and put on a purple robe (φοινικίς) and the crown (στέφανος) of thorns and the reed (κάλαμος) in the hand. Whence, O Celsus, have you learned these, than from the gospels? Did you then see these worthy of reproach (ὀνειδισμός), and those recording (ἀναγράφω) them did not perceive that you and those like you would laugh, but others would take as example (παράδειγμα) of despising those laughing and jeering (χλευάζω) at piety (εὐσέβεια) the one who readily (ἑτοίμως) died for it? Rather marvel at their love of truth (τὸ φιλάληθες) and at the one who suffered these willingly (ἑκουσίως) for men and endured (ὑπομένω) them with all forbearance (ἀνεξικακία) and long-suffering (μακροθυμία); for it was not recorded that he lamented (ὀδύρομαι) or that anything ignoble (ἀγεννής) from being condemned was thought (νομίζω) or uttered (ἀναφθέγγομαι).
pass_b_english: Celsus’s Jew, thinking he is making fun of Jesus, is portrayed as knowing the Bacchus of Euripides, who says, “The god himself will set me free whenever I wish” (Euripides, Bacchae 498). Jews are hardly given to the study of Greek literature. But let it be that some Jew became so well read. How then does it follow that Jesus, because he did not set himself free when bound, could not have done so? Let him believe, from my own Scriptures, that Peter too, bound in prison, came out when an angel loosed his chains (Acts 12:6–10), and that Paul, with Silas, bound in “the stocks” at Philippi in Macedonia, was set free by divine power, when the “doors” of the prison also “were opened” (Acts 16:24–26). But Celsus probably laughs at these things, or else never read the story at all. Otherwise he would have seen fit to answer it by saying that some sorcerers also loose bonds and open doors by incantations, so as to put what sorcerers do on the same level as what is recorded among us.

“But not even the man who condemned him,” he says, “suffered anything like Pentheus, who went mad or was torn apart.” He did not see that it was not so much Pilate who had condemned him, since Pilate “knew that it was out of envy that” the Jews “had handed him over” (Matthew 27:18), as the Jewish nation. That nation has been condemned by God, torn apart and scattered over all the earth, more terribly than Pentheus was torn apart. And why did he deliberately pass over the story of Pilate’s wife, who had seen a dream and was so moved by it that she sent word to her husband and said, “Have nothing to do with this righteous man, for today I have suffered many things in a dream because of him” (Matthew 27:19)?

And again, keeping silent about what reveals the divinity of Jesus, Celsus reproaches him with what is written in the gospel about him, citing those who mocked him and put a crimson cloak on him, the crown of thorns and the reed in his hand (Matthew 27:28–29). Where then, Celsus, did you learn these things, if not from the gospels? Did you, then, see that these things deserved reproach, while those who recorded them did not perceive that you and those like you would laugh, but that others would take him who readily died for piety as an example of how to scorn those who laugh and jeer at them for their piety? Rather, then, marvel at their love of truth, and at him who willingly suffered these things for the sake of men, and endured them with all forbearance and patience. For it is not recorded that he lamented, or that his condemnation drew from him any ignoble thought or word.

choices.why: οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι after the Matthew 27:18 words was dropped; restored as 'the Jews' outside the quotation marks
Matthew 27:19 as Origen gives it has τῷ ἀνθρώπῳ τούτῳ τῷ δικαίῳ: 'that righteous man' changed to 'this righteous man'
ἐπὶ εὐσεβείᾳ: 'jeer at piety' changed to 'jeer at them for their piety' (mockery on account of piety, not mockery of piety)
ἔδοξε γὰρ ἂν λέγειν: 'Otherwise, it seems, he would have answered' changed to 'Otherwise he would have seen fit to answer'
ὑπὲρ τὸν Πενθέως σπαραγμόν: 'beyond the tearing apart of Pentheus' changed to 'more terribly than Pentheus was torn apart'
φοινικίς: 'purple cloak' changed to 'crimson cloak'; 'thinking to make fun' changed to 'thinking he is making fun'; οὖν rendered in 'Rather, then, marvel'
Checked: Euripides, Bacchae 498 exact; Acts 12:6–10; Acts 16:24–26 (ξύλον, θύραι ἠνεῴχθησαν); Matthew 27:18, 27:19, 27:28–29

2.34: ἦ γὰρ at 'Let him believe' looks corrupt (perhaps ἢ γάρ). Translator's counter-demand reading kept; no owner decision needed

2.34: Koetschau's supplied (ἢ) with passive ἐνομίσθη in the last sentence. Rendered 'his condemnation drew from him any ignoble thought or word'; I checked it and it is defensible, but the text is uncertain

translator_notes: Euripides, Bacchae 498 (λύσει μ᾽ ὁ δαίμων αὐτός, ὅταν ἐγὼ θέλω) is quoted exactly. δαίμων here is the pagan god, so lower case. Pentheus’ madness and tearing apart are from the same play, not a quotation, so no line citation. ἦ γὰρ at the start of ‘Let him believe’ is odd in the transmitted text (perhaps ἢ γάρ or εἰ γάρ); sense rendered as a counter-demand, which the context requires. ‘Matthew 27:18’ wording: Origen adds οἱ Ἰουδαῖοι to explain ‘they’; the English keeps ‘the Jews’ outside the quotation marks. Origen’s claim that the Jewish nation, rather than Pilate, condemned Jesus and was itself ‘condemned by God’ is his polemic and is translated as written, with the σπαραχθέν/διασπαρέν wordplay kept as ‘torn apart and scattered’. Last sentence: Koetschau’s supplied (ἢ) and the passive ἐνομίσθη are awkward; taken as ‘that he thought or uttered anything ignoble because of his condemnation’, rendered ‘that his condemnation drew from him any ignoble thought or word’. Mocking scene also in Mark 15:17–19 and John 19:2–3; φοινικίς (a red, purple-red military cloak) sits between Mark’s πορφύρα and Matthew’s χλαμύδα κοκκίνην, so rendered ‘crimson cloak’.
